claims.text: The target material is equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
Processed HfNbTaTiZr typically has a disordered BCC structure.
Additively manufactured HfNbTaTiZr specimens contain approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
HfNbTaTiZr can be produced using additive manufacturing followed by sintering.
The proposed approach separately models anharmonic lattice transport and electronic transport.
The proposed approach represents oxygen defects and disorder rather than assuming a perfect defect-free crystal.
Oxygen interstitials and inherent lattice disorder enhance phonon scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen interstitials do not significantly modify the electronic band structure of HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen point defects and configurational disorder reduce the phonon mean free path.
The reduced phonon mean free path lowers lattice thermal conductivity.
Electronic heat transport is minimally affected by approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Oxygen-induced disorder reduces lattice thermal conductivity by approximately 30% relative to conventional Debye-based estimates.
At approximately 1000 K, lattice thermal conductivity is predicted to be 5 ± 1.5 W/(m·K).
At approximately 1000 K, combining the predicted lattice and electronic contributions gives a total conductivity within 10–17 W/(m·K).
The decoupled method reduces prediction error by more than 30% relative to traditional unified approaches.
The intended applicability range is 300–1200 K for processed, disordered HfNbTaTiZr containing up to approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The hypothesis may not apply to nearly perfect single crystals.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-transport contributions are strongly coupled.
From 300 to 1200 K, phonon anharmonicity dominates the relevant lattice-transport behavior.
Failure to observe the predicted lattice-conductivity reduction within ±2 W/(m·K) at 1000 K, or observation of a significant oxygen-induced electronic change, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions say the method is not applicable below 200 K, whereas the boundary excludes the broader regime below 300 K. The exact lower applicability limit is therefore inconsistent.
